alternative: a runtime state machine - an explicit state field with guarded transitions, or a statechart library such as XState - and TypeScript for the parts whose illegal calls must fail at build time.
idiom_name: none at compile time; runtime state machine (state field + transition table, or XState)
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no static type system, so a state cannot be a type parameter and no transition can be a compile error: JSDoc annotations are erased at run time and cannot enforce call order. What replaces the classic structure is a runtime state machine - keep the state in one field or private slot, declare the legal transitions as data, and reject an illegal event at the boundary; XState turns that into a formal machine with guards and effect handling. Adopting TypeScript for the same machine recovers compile-time checking of event names and payloads, which is the only way to get the typestate guarantee in this ecosystem.
pitfalls: A check that lives in one method is bypassed by any other mutation path; funnel every state change through the transition table.
Private class fields (#state) hide the state but do not enforce sequencing; the runtime check still has to exist.
String event names accept typos until they throw; freeze the tables and, where possible, derive literal union types in TypeScript.
